label: Maintenance becomes the constraint
title: Anyone can write it. Who keeps it running?
thesis: As machine assistance drives the cost of producing a change towards zero, the binding constraint on a software organisation moves to keeping what has already been merged working — and that capacity has not been automated to the same degree. Benchmarks that test sustained maintenance rather than isolated fixes find most agents regress previously passing tests, and repository-level complexity and static-analysis warnings rise persistently after agent adoption rather than as a one-off cost. If this holds, the scarce organisational capability becomes stewardship of merged code — ownership, review depth, and the decision to revisit — rather than the ability to produce more of it. Agents closing the gap between one-shot and sustained performance, or complexity indicators settling back after adoption, would refute it.
construct: What happens to code after it is merged: whether it keeps working, how often it has to be revisited, and how repository-level complexity and defect indicators move as the machine-authored share rises. Not the pass rate of agents on isolated benchmark tasks, not how much code is produced or how fast, not developer-reported productivity, and not the security properties of a single generated snippet — all of which are consistent with a codebase that stays exactly as maintainable as it was.
currentPressure: Repository-level static-analysis warnings and cognitive complexity rise after coding agents are adopted and stay raised, and the field's standard delivery-metrics framework has added a rework measure alongside throughput.

implications.statement: A benchmark running 18 models across 100 codebases over 233 simulated maintenance days found most regress previously passing tests, with only one model series clearing a 50% zero-regression rate — so performance on one-shot fixes says little about the cost the same agent imposes over a codebase's life, and procurement evidence and operating evidence are not the same evidence.

Static-analysis warnings rose about 18% and cognitive complexity about 39% after agent adoption, persistently and regardless of prior AI tooling, so the work of holding complexity down has to be scheduled as continuous load rather than treated as cleanup after a push.

A survival analysis across 201 projects found agent-authored code is modified less often than human-written code, which means durable machine-authored code can become a long-lived dependency that nobody has read — making explicit ownership a maintenance control rather than a bureaucratic one.
Throughput and rework move in opposite directions in the same dataset, so a delivery dashboard reporting only throughput reports a gain that the rework line is already spending.

evidence.note: 18 models across 100 real codebases over 233 simulated maintenance days: agents break previously passing tests in roughly 75% of cases, and only the Claude Opus series clears a 50% zero-regression rate. Measures sustained upkeep rather than one-shot fixes.

Repository-level comparison of autonomous agents against AI IDE tooling: static-analysis warnings up ~18% and cognitive complexity up ~39%, persistent across settings rather than a one-off adoption cost.
~110,000 open-source pull requests across five agents: agent-authored code is significantly more likely to be rewritten, reverted or substantially modified in later commits.

~5,000 survey responses plus 100+ hours of interviews: AI raises delivery throughput while raising instability and rework, and the report adds Rework Rate as a formal metric alongside the existing four.

Survival analysis of 200,000+ code units across 201 projects finds agent-authored code is modified LESS often than human-written code — a 15.8 percentage-point lower modification rate, HR 0.842 — which is the opposite direction from the churn study above on the same question. The authors nonetheless conclude the constraint is the practices governing evolution rather than generation quality.

142,652 agentic pull requests across 59,412 repositories: 27.67% hit merge conflicts, averaging 11.36 conflict regions and ~540 conflicting lines. The authors explicitly decline the comparison with human-authored baselines, so this measures the integration cost without showing it has grown.

reachRationale: The measurements are population-scale and independent of one another — 18 models across 100 codebases over simulated maintenance cycles, 201 open-source projects, roughly 110,000 pull requests, and a survey of about 5,000 practitioners — and the field's standard delivery-metrics framework has responded by adding a rework measure, which is an institution changing what it counts. What has not happened is organisations reorganising around it: the same survey reports throughput being pursued regardless, and nothing in the evidence shows procurement or staffing decisions being made on sustained-maintenance evidence rather than on one-shot performance. The argument for the centre is that a change to the canonical delivery-metric set is itself a field-level marker; a reviewer who weighs that more heavily than the absence of organisational response should move this inwards.
whatWouldChangeThis: A sustained-maintenance benchmark shows agents closing the gap with their one-shot performance across model families, not just one
Repository complexity and static-analysis warnings settle back towards pre-adoption levels once teams have a year of agent use behind them
The churn disagreement resolves in favour of agent code being more durable, and the corrective-churn premium disappears with it
Organisations begin selecting and staffing on sustained-maintenance evidence, which would make this an accepted operating fact rather than a claim about where the constraint is heading
